newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam seeks to dampen devaluation talk.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam seeks to dampen devaluation talk.

text.p: Vietnam moved on Monday to dampen speculation over a devaluation of its currency, the dong, by denying the move in a series of media statements, but foreign bankers said the market was still confused.

In an interview with the Lao Dong (Labour) newspaper, State Bank Governor Cao Si Kiem was quoted as saying no devaluation was planned and the policy of the bank was to maintain a stable exchange rate.
He added, however, that the exchange rates were being adjusted according to demand and supply.
"I haven't got a clue what's going on," said one foreign banker, who declined to be identified. "And I'm not alone."

Kiem's comments were the latest in a series by State Bank officials seeking to restore exchange rate stability, which until this month had seen the dong virtually unchanged at around 11,000 to the dollar since 1994.
On Monday the dong was steady at around 11,054 to the dollar. Local newspapers reported last week a black market rate of 11,300 in Ho Chi Minh City.
"I think some of the reason there's been confusion is perhaps with the use of the words devaluation and depreciation," said treasury analyst Peter McLean of Standard Chartered Bank in Hanoi.
"I'm seeing this as a continuation of the policy of depreciation -- in other words a stable movement in one direction," he said.

McLean said Vietnam's State Bank had been aiming at a gradual depreciation for the past three years but had been unable to achieve it primarily because the inflow of dollars had been greater than the outflow requirement.
"It may be speeded up a little in terms of depreciation, simply because there's an opportunity in the market to do that at the moment, but I don't see any devaluation," McLean said.

Bankers said the current interbank market in Vietnam was illiquid. They said possible factors behind this could include a slowdown in the inflow of foreign investment inflow capital and a growing volume of imports.
Mclean said he was expecting the dong to trade in the range 11025-70 to the dollar for the remainder of this year with a likely one percent per quarter depreciation in 1997.
"They have tried for three years to create confidence in the dong, and now they have got to make sure that people feel safe and happy to use the dong," he said.
